headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ms-swift can read/write files and call external APIs, while awesome-prompts is a prompt repository with no isolation or verification boundary.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt/content repository, and ms-swift can read files and consume stdin/stdout plus API outputs. If ms-swift ingests prompt files from a shared workspace, attacker-controlled prompt text could steer downstream behavior. The pair lacks documented isolation or provenance controls, so the interaction is plausible in default CLI workflows.
conditions: IF ms-swift reads prompt files from the same workspace as awesome-prompts content
IF prompt text from awesome-prompts is passed into ms-swift without provenance tagging
mitigations: Store prompt repositories in a read-only directory
Require manual review before feeding prompt files into ms-swift
Prefix imported text with provenance labels
Use separate workspaces for prompt sources and execution
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts itself shows no data classes touched and no egress, but ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and secrets and can call external APIs. If both share a workspace, files from the prompt repo or adjacent artifacts can be exposed through ms-swift's file access and outbound API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF awesome-prompts content is placed in a workspace readable by ms-swift
IF ms-swift is configured to send file contents or logs to allowlisted external APIs
mitigations: Keep prompt assets outside ms-swift input directories
Disable upload of logs and artifacts where possible
Use separate OS users for the two agents
Review allowlisted endpoints before execution
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts is non-runnable and has no write capabilities, while ms-swift can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. There is no direct write-write conflict, but both can operate on shared files if co-located, creating overwrite or corruption risk in default CLI workflows. Uncertainty remains because ms-swift's shared-state behavior is not stated.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF ms-swift writes outputs into paths also used by prompt assets or logs
mitigations: Use distinct output directories
Mount the prompt repository read-only
Run ms-swift under a separate OS account
Avoid concurrent writes to shared paths
requires-engineering: add file locking or workspace partitioning

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts provides prompt content, and ms-swift can execute CLI/Python workflows that may treat imported text as authoritative instructions or configuration. If ms-swift consumes repository prompts without verification, errors or malicious instructions can cascade into generated outputs, logs, or downstream API actions. The lack of documented verification increases uncertainty, so the higher severity is chosen.
conditions: IF ms-swift uses awesome-prompts content as templates or system prompts
IF generated text from awesome-prompts is forwarded into automated scripts or API calls
mitigations: Require human review of imported prompts
Separate prompt generation from execution steps
Log source provenance for every imported prompt
Test with a non-production workspace first
requires-engineering: add validation gates before action-taking

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented for either agent, and awesome-prompts appears to be a content repository with no data classes touched. ms-swift does handle secrets and can call external APIs, so compliance risk exists only if regulated data is routed through it. Because the relevant mismatch is not evidenced, this remains low rather than medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through ms-swift
IF external API endpoints used by ms-swift are outside the operator's approved residency or DPA boundary
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through ms-swift
Confirm approved endpoints before use
Keep secrets out of prompt repositories
Review retention settings for logs and outputs
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
